summary: The Server/Application State Protocol lets load balancers and workload managers communicate better ways to spread work across a group of systems. Work distributors usually know little about how well applications can finish work, and health monitors have little control over how much arrives. SASP bridges that gap. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: A person handing out jobs does not know who is tired. This protocol lets the workers tell the job-giver how busy they are, so jobs are shared more fairly.

questions: how do load balancers learn server load
how does load balancer know server capacity
how does workload manager communicate with load balancer
subtitle: Letting load balancers know how busy each server really is.

tldr.problem: Load balancers and workload managers have conflicting knowledge: load balancers know where requests come from but not how busy their servers are, while workload managers know server health but cannot control work distribution.
tldr.mechanism: SASP is a binary protocol over TCP/TLS in which workload managers report weight recommendations to load balancers and managers can register or request information about group members and their current capacity.
tldr.outcome: Load balancers can distribute work more fairly according to actual server capacity rather than guessing, improving utilization and preventing overload.

today: RFC 4678 is an Informational document from September 2006 and has never been updated or obsoleted. The protocol remains a vendor-specific solution for workload management; it was not adopted as a standard and is primarily used in proprietary load balancing systems.

sections.title: The Load Balancing Problem
sections.content:
Load balancers are the gatekeepers of distributed systems. They take incoming requests and forward them to a group of equivalent servers. But here is their limitation: they know the request volume they are sending to each server, but not how well those servers can actually handle the work. Some servers might be fast or idle; others might be overloaded with background tasks.

Meanwhile, workload managers (often called health monitors or orchestration systems) actually observe how busy each server is, but they have no way to influence the load balancer's decisions. SASP closes this gap by creating a conversation between the two.
sections.eli5: Load balancers are like store managers sending customers to different checkout counters, but they do not know which clerks are tired. Workload managers watch the clerks closely but cannot tell the manager to redirect people. SASP lets them talk.

sections.title: Message Structure and Types
sections.content:
SASP sends binary messages over a long-lived TCP connection secured with TLS. Every message starts with a header containing the protocol version, message length and a message ID that helps match replies to requests.

The actual content of each message uses a TLV (Type, Length, Value) format. Each component has a 2-byte type field (saying what kind of data it is), a 2-byte length field (the size in bytes), and a variable-length value. This design makes it easy to add new attribute types in the future without breaking old implementations.

There are six main kinds of messages: Registration (telling the workload manager about new members), DeRegistration (removing members), Get Weights (asking for load recommendations), Send Weights (reporting new weights), and two state-setting messages that let applications and load balancers signal their current condition.
sections.eli5: Every message is a labeled box with a size tag and contents. The load balancer can ask the workload manager "who are my members" or "what weights should I use," and the manager can say "this server is tired, use less" or "this one crashed, forget about it."

sections.title: Actors and Their Roles
sections.content:
SASP involves three kinds of entities:

The Load Balancer (LB) is the entity that makes routing decisions. It connects to the workload manager and registers its groups of servers, asks for weight recommendations, and updates the workload manager about what is happening.

Group Members are the actual application servers. They may register themselves with the workload manager to announce they are ready to receive work, or the load balancer can register them. Members also report their current state (e.g., "I am busy right now").

The Group Workload Manager (GWM) is the central authority. It listens for TCP connections from load balancers and members. It collects information about member health and capacity, computes recommendations, and sends weight values back. Members are identified by IP address, transport protocol (TCP or UDP), and port number.
sections.eli5: There are three roles: the load balancer (who sends out jobs), the servers (who do the jobs), and the manager (who watches how busy everyone is and makes suggestions).

sections.title: Weights and Member State
sections.content:
The core idea of SASP is the weight: a number from 0 to 65,535 that represents how much work a load balancer should send to a member relative to the others. A weight of 100 means twice as much work as a weight of 50. Zero means avoid that member entirely.

The workload manager assigns weights based on what it observes: member health, CPU usage, memory pressure, pending tasks, or vendor-specific metrics. Each weight entry also includes flags that tell the load balancer important things: whether the member is running, whether it is deliberately quiesced (temporarily paused for maintenance), whether the manager is confident in its assessment, and whether the member registered itself or was registered by the load balancer.

Members can also send their own state information to indicate they are getting overloaded and should be quiesced, or that they are ready to accept more work.
sections.eli5: The manager assigns each server a number saying "send this server twice as much work as that one" or "this server is tired, send it zero." Flags let the manager say "I am watching this server" or "I just took it offline for repairs."

sections.title: What Happens in Practice
sections.content:
A typical SASP interaction works like this: A load balancer connects to the workload manager and proposes a protocol version (usually 1). The manager accepts if it supports that version, or suggests a lower version if needed.

The load balancer then registers one or more groups, each with a name and a set of member IP addresses, ports, and protocols. The workload manager acknowledges and may assign initial weights.

At intervals, the load balancer asks "Get Weights" and the workload manager replies with an updated weight for each member. The load balancer then adjusts its distribution accordingly. If a member crashes or recovers, the workload manager sends new weights. If the load balancer wants to take a member offline temporarily, it sends a Set Member State message with the quiesce flag on, and the workload manager zeroes that member's weight.

The document includes detailed examples showing load balancer registration, getting weights, application-side state changes, and error handling.
sections.eli5: The load balancer says "I have these three servers." The manager watches them and says "send twice as much to server 1, half to server 2, and none to server 3 because it crashed." The load balancer uses those numbers to route new requests fairly.
